# On the Peculiar Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about how we move through the world mostly blind to it. Not blind in any literal sense—our eyes work fine, scanning faces and screens and the path ahead. But there's a deeper blindness, a learned incuriosity that makes us see without really *seeing*. I notice this especially in myself when I'm in a hurry, which is almost always. The coffee cup becomes merely a vessel for caffeine. The commute becomes merely time to endure. The person sitting across from me becomes merely someone whose turn it is to talk while I wait to talk.

This seems like a disease of modernity, though I suspect people have always struggled with this problem. The farmer probably looked at the same field for forty years and stopped seeing it around year two. The fisherman's wife probably stopped noticing the smell of the sea. We habituate. We adjust. We stop marveling. This is efficient, I suppose. Useful. But something gets lost.

I've started collecting small observations, trying to rewild my attention a little. Nothing profound—just moments where something ordinary suddenly seems strange and beautiful if you really look at it.

Consider the human hand. I know, I know—artists have been waxing rhapsodic about hands forever. But that's actually my point. They're not waxing rhapsodic to be pretentious. Hands are genuinely, almost offensively perfect in their design. The way the thumb opposes the other fingers, allowing us to grip and manipulate and create. The specific musculature that lets someone play a cello or a video game, type a love letter or a grocery list. The scars and calluses and wrinkles that tell stories. We mostly just use them without thought, moving them through space like we move our eyes, as if they're magic that needs no explanation.

When I actually *look* at a hand—someone else's or my own—I'm struck by how much of human civilization is possible because of this particular configuration of bones and tendons and skin. Not just the physical things we've built, but everything we've created: music, art, writing, cooking, the specific comfort of holding someone's hand. A hand reaching out. A hand held out in greeting. A hand covering a mouth in surprise. The vocabulary of human touch wouldn't exist without this remarkable piece of biological engineering.

Or think about water. This is embarrassing—I'm embarrassed even writing it—but I was struck recently by the fact that water is transparent. Like, I *know* water is transparent. I use it every day, bathe in it, drink it. But sometimes I'll be pouring water into a glass and actually consider what I'm looking at: a liquid that lets light pass through it. It's such a specific and valuable property, and it's *everywhere*, and we barely notice. We notice when something blocks our vision, but perfect clarity? Invisibility? We take it for granted.

My sister sent me a video recently of her daughter—my niece—who is four years old, discovering that she can see her hand through a glass of water. Not that the glass of water was particularly magnifying, just that she was seeing her hand in a completely different medium, and it had that slight warping to it, and she was absolutely astonished. She kept moving her hand and giggling. She must have done it for five minutes straight, and her mother said she came back to it multiple times that day. It was, to her, the most incredible discovery.

I wonder when we lose that. When does watching light refract through water stop being astonishing and become just something water does? First grade? High school? Sometime in adulthood when we've decided that novelty only belongs to genuinely new experiences?

I've been trying to recapture that sometimes. Looking at the way light hits a puddle. Watching the specific way someone's face changes when they're really listening to something that matters to them. Noticing the complex geometry of a tree, the way branches split and split again, each segment following the same mathematical principle but always ending up looking slightly different.

There's a tree outside my window—I've walked past it maybe five thousand times—and last week I really *looked* at it. It's a birch tree. I don't know exactly which species, but it's the kind with papery white bark that peels. The winter had worn it, left bare branches reaching up, and I noticed that each branch has this series of small dark marks on it, like the spots on a leopard. I pulled out my phone to look it up, because I had to know if there was a name for those marks, if there was a reason they were there. (Apparently they're lenticels, pores that let the tree breathe. Of course. Everything has a reason.)

This is the weird thing about really looking: once you start noticing the detail and the reason and the mechanism, it somehow becomes even more interesting rather than less. You'd think that understanding would drain the mystery out of something. But somehow it doesn't. Knowing that those marks are how a tree breathes doesn't make the pattern less beautiful. If anything, it makes the tree seem more alive, more intentional in its design.

I think this is why people develop hobbies and obsessions. Birders don't spend hours in the woods because birds are merely birds. Aquarium enthusiasts aren't just keeping fish alive. Gardeners aren't just growing food. They're all doing the same thing: they're choosing to look closely at something, to let it become complicated and detailed and endlessly interesting. They're choosing not to habituate.

And it strikes me that this might be one of the deepest sources of meaning available to us, if we wanted it. Not in the grand sense—not necessarily in major life achievements or relationships (though those matter too). But the smaller, granular meaning of *actually paying attention*. Of noticing. Of letting the world be strange and detailed and specific rather than blurring it into categories and generalizations.

There's a restaurant I like, a small place run by a woman named Claire who's probably in her sixties. She's been making the same menu items for twenty years, and she makes them impeccably. But what I've noticed is that she seems genuinely interested in each plate of food she prepares, even though she must have made the same dish a thousand times. She's not just assembling ingredients. She's arranging them carefully. She's thinking about how it looks and tastes and sits on the plate. 

I asked her once if she didn't get bored, making the same ten dishes forever. She looked at me like I'd asked if she gets bored by breathing. "Every tomato is different," she said. "Different season, different soil. Every person who comes in is different, so you're making the same dish but for a different person, so it's not the same at all." 

That's stuck with me. Every tomato is different. Which seems obvious once you think about it, but it means that no dish is ever quite repeated. Every moment of cooking is genuinely novel, if you're paying attention.

I think the older I get, the more I realize that this is what separates a life that feels rich from one that feels empty: not what happens to you, but whether you're actually *there* for what happens to you. Whether you're really experiencing it, or whether you're just moving through it on autopilot, checking boxes, waiting for the real part of your life to start.

The real part never starts, by the way. Or rather, it's always already started. It's happening now, in this moment, whatever moment you're reading this in. The light in your room right now will never exist exactly this way again. The specific configuration of things around you is unique. The thoughts in your head are completely your own. This moment will never come back.

This sounds like I'm building toward something inspirational, like "so live each day as if it were your last" or some sort of motivational poster sentiment. But I don't think it needs to be quite so dramatic. I'm not suggesting we should approach every moment with reverent intensity. That would be exhausting. More like: occasionally pause. Notice something small. Become interested in something for its own sake, with no utility involved. Let yourself be surprised by the ordinary.

Because the ordinary is actually extraordinary if you look at it properly. A coffee cup holds hot liquid against gravity, contains temperature through careful material engineering. A morning commute is a journey through space taken by a biological being so complex that scientists still don't fully understand how it works. Someone sitting across from you is a person who experiences the world from completely inside their own head, whose inner life is as real and complex as yours, whom you can never fully know despite living in the same reality. These aren't small things.

I've been trying to write about attention and wonder for a while now, and I keep coming back to the same conclusion: we've got it backwards. We treat ordinary things as boring and commonplace when they're actually endlessly interesting if we just look. And we treat extraordinary things—vacations, accomplishments, rare experiences—as if they're the only things worth paying attention to. But the truth is that everything is extraordinary. A cup of tea. A person's face in different light. The sound of rain. The way a dog's whole body gets involved in wagging its tail, not just the tail. The texture of bread crust. The first moment you realize someone finds you funny, the split second of connection when humor clicks.

I think the greatest tragedy of modern life might not be that bad things happen, but that good things happen all the time and we're too distracted or habituated to notice. We walk through gardens and don't see the flowers. We eat beautiful food without tasting it. We talk to people we love while thinking about our phone. We're surrounded by small miracles and we're too preoccupied to care.

So I'm trying to reverse-engineer the child's attention, to become like that four-year-old with the glass of water. Not in a naive way—I don't need to pretend I don't understand physics to be fascinated by it. But to let myself be astonished by how things work, how things are designed, how someone looks when they're lost in thought, how the light changes through the day, how every single thing is exactly as strange as I'm willing to look at.

The good news is that this doesn't require anything special. No expense, no travel, no achievement. Just a choice to look. To really look. To let yourself be interested. To notice that the ordinary is already extraordinary, if you pay attention.
